title: The mustard seed and the yeast (Matthew 13:31–33)
hookLine: the kingdom starts smaller than you'd notice and works through everything

lines: THIS IS WHAT THE KINGDOM IS LIKE?
cards: Hold a mustard seed on your fingertip and you'll barely see it. Drop it on the kitchen floor and you'll never find it again. Then there's a small lump of yeast, a spoonful of old dough from yesterday's bread.
You wouldn't look at either one twice. And that's what Jesus reaches for to say what the kingdom of heaven is like. Not a palace.
Not an army. Not a thunderclap. A seed you could lose, and a bit of dough a woman hides in the flour.
Two parables, three verses between them.

teach.b: The first, in the Douay-Rheims: "The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field."
The least of all the seeds, Jesus says, but when it's grown it becomes a tree, and the birds of the air come and live in its branches.
Some scholars point out that mustard is also a bit of a weed: once it's in your field, it spreads. On that reading, the kingdom isn't neat. It takes over.

The second parable is one sentence long: "The kingdom of heaven is like to leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." Leaven isn't the packet kind of yeast.
It was a lump of old, sour dough kept back from the last batch. And look at the verb: she hid it. You can't see it working.
Three measures of meal, some readers reckon, is enough to bake bread for a crowd. One small hidden lump, and the whole mass rises.
Two pictures, one idea: in these parables, the kingdom starts too small to notice, works out of sight, and goes all the way through. Catholics have a saint known for this.
Thérèse of Lisieux, a young Carmelite nun, called her path the little way: doing ordinary, tiny things with great love.
The Church later named her a Doctor of the Church.

how: Catholics hear these parables at Sunday Mass in summer, and many take up Saint Thérèse of Lisieux's little way, doing small daily tasks with great love as a path of holiness.

games.q: someone asks you to describe the kingdom of heaven in one picture. what does Jesus choose?
o: a great king on a throne.
a seed so small you could lose it.
a mighty army on the march.
games.why: a mustard seed, and then a lump of leaven hidden in flour. small, hidden, and working all the way through.

practice: Let your day come to mind, hour by hour, and find a place in it for one very small good thing: a kind word to the person at the register, a text that says thinking of you, a cup put away that isn't yours.
Not a project, a seed; pick one and see yourself doing it, and don't mind that it won't look like much, because it isn't supposed to. If you pray, you can offer it to God in advance.

wordCard.voice: leaven. An old lump of sour dough, hidden in the flour until the whole batch rises, the kingdom's small, hidden work.

orig.note: Greek: leaven, a lump of fermented dough kept back to start the next batch.

carryVoice: Your line: small is how it starts. The whole batch rises from one hidden lump. See you tomorrow.
